One common strategy to implement active learning is with group work. (Emily, 
et al., 2024) conducted a meta-analysis looking into the effectiveness of group 
work within the classroom. With groups of at least two or more students, they 
found that the student academic performance significantly increased by an 
average of one standard deviation. The paper states that the following reasons 
contribute towards group works success: (1) collaboration and knowledge 
sharing, (2) accountability and motivation, (3) increased feedback to address 
misconceptions from peers. 
Another approach is to gamify the learning experience, (Deterding, et al., 2011; 
Sailer & Homner, 2019) defines gamification as the inclusion of game elements 
such as badges or scores, to a non-game context. In a meta-analysis by (Sailer 
& Homner, 2019), showed that there was a small but significant positive affect 
towards learning goals and student motivation when compared to passive and 
other active learning strategies. Some implemented aspects that contributed 
towards the success of gamification included: (1) the element of self-
determination theory, (2) gamified feedback elements such as scores, and (3) 
social aspects such as collaboration or competition. 
To conclude, active learning is an effective teaching methodology at provoking 
higher level cognitive function, by requiring students to think in more detail. The 
teaching methodology allows students to explore what they have learned; and 
enables students to create and challenge their new and existing ideas. Active 
learning in a social context seemed to be a highly affective and common choice 
among the analysed research papers; despite this there is little research on the 
most effective strategies such as interactive lectures, gamification, and 
socialisation.
